en: In the *Rājatarangiṇī* by Jonarāja and Pseudo-Jonarāja: When Siddha was present there, Śeṣa— honored by the three worlds— bore his own two halves within himself as if agitated by shame due to the loss of his desire for rivalry.
May that union of the two halves of the Lord’s body—meeting so closely as if longing to conquer the two internal organs that have become one through affection—be for the attainment of true being.
May that king of the Gaṇas, who is pot-bellied as if daily carrying within him auspiciousness to bestow upon his devotee, grant us the pacification of obstacles.
It is said that from the time of Śrī Gonanda onwards, until the end of the Kali age, the land of Kaśmīra was protected by kings who were devoted to the Dharma and abounding in virtues.
While the darkness of the winter night of their misfortune persisted,
no one at all beheld them for a long time, as the sun of Kāvya had not yet risen.

Then the poet Kalhaṇa caused his own fame— ending with the illustrious Jayasiṃha— to attain eternal youthfulness by means of speech composed of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which had already brought old age upon the [previous] chronicle.
Then, due to defects in the region and so forth, or perhaps because of his own misfortune,
a certain poet did not sustain others with the nectar of his speech before rival kings.
While the illustrious Jainaullābhadīna now protects the earth without injury, I,
named Jonarāja, am diligent in describing their history.
This tree of poetry has been planted to destroy the continuous heat of the travelers who are kings— a heat born of the exhaustion of pride— and it shall yield the emergence of future fruit.
Having added the essence of refinement, this [work] should be further nourished with great effort by virtuous people who are cooled by the nectar of discipline.
These great kings of the past, who had sunk into the ocean of oblivion,
were sought to be rescued through the compassion of the illustrious Jaiñollābhadīna.
Having received the command from the mouth of Śrī Śirya Bhaṭṭa— who was compassionate and appointed to all matters of state— with due respect, [he acted].
My present inspiration is for the purpose of completing the royal chronicle;
it is not out of a desire for the fame of being a poet that I am making this effort.
Where is my speech, which is like water mixed with cumin, and where is poetry, which is rippled with aesthetic waves?
How could a reed ever act like a lotus, merely by imitating its shadow?
Carrying this light wisdom, hollow within like a gourd,
alas, I have set out to cross to the further shore of the River of Kings.
In my contemplation of the virtues of the Lord of the Earth, my restlessness is no fault;
for even an ugly woman moves with grace when adorned with ornaments out of self-confidence.
Or perhaps my speech may be useful to poets for the purification of their own inner selves—
just as the water of the Gaṅgā is for those who have not drunk any other water.
I have merely laid the foundation for this thread of royal narrative;
let the clever artisans among poets now carry out its composition.
The skill of the great whetstone lies only in the grinding of jewels;
but in the bestowing of luster upon them, that belongs to the supreme jewel of the face.
The virtuous behold the poem of a poet even without being requested;
for does the moon drench the entire world with its essence of nectar only when asked?
Even when conciliated, a wicked person does not relinquish his turbidity toward poetry;
even when washed with nectar, charcoal never attains whiteness.
"Let them see my poetry"— this long-standing torment of the poet’s wretchedness, consisting in his looking toward the faces of others for approval, has now vanished far away.
The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of those unskilled in the refinements of song may appear uniform;
like monkeys who, in the cold, pick up *guñjā* berries under the delusion that they are sparks of fire.
Even when heard, poetry brings delight only to those whose minds are not struck by ignorance;
what can sugarcane do when placed in the mouth of one who lacks teeth and strength?
When this poem, beautiful in its meaning, is presented to those of pure soul,
the reflection of envy— the gem of faults— is difficult to restrain.
By defiling the moon with the consumption of jealousy toward Budha because of Lakṣmaṇā,
the Creator incurs reproach as the foremost of those unable to endure the excellence of others.
May my speech attain the savor of being included within the poem of Kalhaṇa; for is not the water of a reed-bed, once fallen into the waters of a river, ever drunk? JRt_26 //
1) Jayasiṃha (reigned 4203–4230), the delight of the world, who was honored by gods and the twice-born,
the illustrious son of Sussala, was a veritable Indra upon the earth.
Bearing even the renown of being borne solely by the king of elephants,
it is a marvel that the Goddess Śrī always dwelt within him who was named Jayasiṃha.
While the king was cherished by the Goddess of Speech and enjoyed the fortune of his mother,
no conflict was perceived between those two, as they stood in the relationship of mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.
The king accepted Malla, who had been under the control of Suśarman, the lord of Trigarta; he had been driven away by his enemies and had arrived seeking a livelihood.
Everywhere, ordinary people— even those who have traveled to distant lands— regard all medicinal herbs, grasses, gems, and even stones as possessing virtues,

so long as they do not bring before them a person who is stainless, expansive, and capable of delighting others through deeds that proclaim the excellence of what is worthy of longing and through states of being full of wonders.
When Vasudhāvāsava had departed to conquer the land of the Yavanas,
a wrestler became the favorite of the army due to his excess of valor.
At night, Mallacandra, exulting in his valor, went to the enemy camp to confront the remnants of the Turuṣka army that had survived the slaughter.
Where the wind did not enter, as if out of fear, for it was surrounded by great warriors;
surely, having entered that army through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, [the wind remained there].
Fearing the sin of treachery against one who was asleep, he did not kill the Yavana lord;
instead, he took his two shoes, marked with his own name, and made them his helmet.
Then that enemy, having recognized and taken the two sandals,
went to the king's camp and seized his fortune as if it were his fame.

The sun and fire are two forms of Śambhu, as are the moon and water; alas, the world follows blindly from one to the other, weighing them against each other like the sun and moon with corresponding stones. Yet, people who lack discernment fail to perceive their supreme distinction, which consists in qualities that are unique to each and cannot be found in the other.
In his thirtieth year, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna,
that beloved of the earth greatly delighted the eyes of celestial women with his own good fortune.
2) Paramāṇuka (JR 4230–4240):
Then his son, Paramāṇuka, was consecrated by the dull-witted [ministers], just as the *kunda* flower is [anointed] by the petals of the *māgha* season, which are even thinner than atoms. JRt_39 //
Having cast aside the protection of his subjects and disregarded his conquest of the quarters,
the king began, without weariness, the accumulation of his treasury.
Like the wealth of a Vedic scholar who is incapable of either giving or enjoying it,
the two rogues Prayāga and Janaka plundered the king’s fortune.

For those two, having been deprived of their own servants, caused him to be terrified night after night by means of various deeds performed by their subordinates who had taken on the forms of rākṣasas.
Acting out his self-deception,
those two wicked ministers made the king squander his wealth under the pretext that it was for the protection of his life.
Having thus instructed his attendant in the presence of the physician,
he had those two worshipped on the full moon day of Caitra with great jewels covered by grass.
Furthermore, having made his appointment, while the people were looking on,
he offered a blessing to the king and went to the forest at night, adorned with ornaments.
Having accepted the offering from you, Bhiṣāyaka and Vyadhita uttered blessings; they said to the king, "Your kingdom shall be free from obstacles."
On the day of the physician, having made that physician their own servant and having honored him with jewels, they led him into the forest and then released him.
"Kubera, being pleased with you today, adorned with various jewels,
has bestowed his blessing upon you before the eyes of the world and then vanished."
Having spoken thus, the two rogues made the foolish and wretched king grant them their favor.
Thus, having displayed such terrors like a child's, those two rakes plundered the treasury of this Lord Kadu until it was entirely emptied.
Having enjoyed the earth for nine years and ten days,
the king met his end on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhas in his fortieth year.
3) In the forty-seventh year, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the son of that man named Vantideva passed away. JRt_49 //
4) Voppadeva (LS 4247–4256):
The citizens, because they could find no one more suitable, made the man named Voppadeva their king;
he was brought [to power] like a physician who has been honored with a meal of fodder.
Seeing the massive rock, the fool was delighted and then commanded his ministers:
"Let the others be nourished by the drinking of breast milk."
Having heard of the greatness of that place, the fool, together with his ministers,
arrived at the field of Sureśvarī by means of a boat, never having traveled there by land before.
As he made a grimace at his own reflection in the water and struck it with a slap in anger, his jeweled ring fell away.
When the king asked, "Where is the jeweled ring? he replied as follows, drawing a line in the water as a sign of recognition: "It fell there into the water."
Having thus become an example for fools,
he ruled as king for nine years, four months, and two and a half days.
5) Then his younger brother, Jassaka (LS 4256–4274), though unwilling to bear the burden of the earth, was consecrated by the ignorant Lavanys who desired their own advancement.
They are not bound like parrots who repeat the words they have heard;
nor do they suffer the grinding and crushing of the earth, like a field of gravel;
nor are they ever reduced to powder by being crushed, like a stone from the Sindhava region.
For some who possess virtues, even a fault arises for the sake of a great virtue.
The two brothers of that king, brahmins named Kṣuka and Bhīma,
soon transgressed his command out of their habitual roguery.
"Though they were both capable and possessed of great power, how could he endure us?
Even though they recognized the king as full of indignation, these two did not choose anyone else."
And as for the fact that one of those two did not personally enjoy royal splendor,
the cause was his being overflowing with beauty, rather than any apprehension regarding impropriety.
In this regard, the cause is the fear of the Lord of Beauty (Kāma), and not a lack of propriety;
for they go to the embrace of his limbs unrestrained, marking their passion by displaying it in their hearts and causing a trembling to arise.
Alas, what a pity! Wicked pustules, having gained their confidence, especially afflict young women with the agony of poison.
Because her power had been diminished by old age, even her own daughter-in-law, having become disenchanted,
quickly killed Kṣemaka with poison and compelled Bhīma to enjoy her.
Having become marked with white leprosy through her association with the king,
she dispelled her own sin by means of gifts to Mādhava and others.
Having ruled the earth for eighteen years and thirteen days,
he met his end on the tenth day of the final [fortnight] of the month of Māgha in the year 454 of the Yuga era.
6) Jagadeva (LS 4274–4289): Then his son, the illustrious Jagadeva, who was exalted by his discipline,
spread even greater joy among the people, like the month of Madhu.
There, the simultaneous presence of servants who were mutually antagonistic occurred like that of blue and white lotuses at the moment of twilight's arrival.
The lord of the earth, possessed of vast skill in discernment,
extracted that which was ill-situated upon the ground, just as a surgeon extracts a thorn.
Afflicted by the thorn of mental anguish, that king of extraordinary virtue was banished from the lands by his ministers through the power of a conspiracy.
He obtained as a minister and friend one who knew mantras capable of both punishment and favor, and who was a treasury of virtues, just as Rāghava obtained the lord of monkeys.
Then, out of a desire for prosperity, the Sun and the Lord of the Twice-born went together to the land of Kaśmīra; those two were truly wondrous.
Unable to renounce the prosperity they had long enjoyed, the enemies prepared for battle; yet, within the fire of the power of his mantras, they met their end like moths.
Having conquered the earth, the king enjoyed royal fortune that mocked with its parasol and fly-whisks;
but Śrīguṇākara’s son Rāhula enjoyed the fortune of one who was not a king.
In the city of Rajapura, the king, whose desires were fulfilled, constructed for Harṣeśvara a temple adorned with a royal silver parasol.
Then, because of his favoritism, the wicked-minded Padma obtained the position of gatekeeper and subsequently killed the king by administering poisoned food under the guise of a hidden dose.
Having protected the earth for fourteen years, six months, and three days,
he met his end on the fourteenth day of the final fortnight of the month of Caitra in the year eight hundred and nine of the Nanda era.
7) Rājadeva (LS 4289–4312):
Then his son, Rājadeva, fled to Kāṣṭhavāṭa out of fear;
he was brought back by the enemies of the Lord of the Gate stationed on the left side.
Padma, acting with wicked intent, surrounded him— who had entered the fortress called Salhaṇā— with his forces, like a snake encircled by magic circles.
And a certain Caṇḍāla, out of curiosity at seeing the unprecedented sandals brought as a gift,
killed the gatekeeper in battle while he was distracted.
Then, having been consecrated by the priests amidst the sounding of kettledrums and conchs,
he received his servants after the infinite number of subordinate vassals had bowed down before him.
That sovereign of the earth, whose majesty was uniquely unrivaled among lords of beauty, assigned him the status of a resident householder,
thereby entrusting him with the full weight of his responsibilities.
The immensely radiant Narasiṃha brought about the shattering of the pride of those who were wild with beauty, just as fire does for forests.
Although the wrestlers seized half the sovereignty of the illustrious city from the powerful Laṅkeśvara, who was like a moon of great strength, they were not able to prevail over him.
Then Balāḍhyacandra, possessed of intense splendor, established a monastery within the city— a mass of merit that seemed as if it had become incarnate and was marked with his own name.
"Who is this soft Khaśa being consecrated by us? O masters, you have long disregarded the king without consulting him. JRt_83 |||
"I am not a Bhaṭṭa! I am not a Bhaṭṭa! I am not a Bhaṭṭa!"—these words were even heard from the Bhaṭṭas when the plundering of the Bhaṭṭas was announced.
At that very time, in the Śaka year marked by the sky, the arrows, and the nine (950), the teacher Vimala dispelled the confusion regarding the intercalary month of the sixth lunar month.
Free from possessiveness, that moon among kings— Rājadeva, who had accumulated auspicious merit since birth— constructed Rājapurī as well as Rājolaka.
Having protected the earth for twenty-seven days, twenty-three years, and three months, that king met his end.
8) Saṅgrāmadeva (LS 4312–4328): That son of Saṅgrāmadeva, who possessed the lineage of Sutrāman (Indra), was a lion among kings; he instilled terror in the elephants of his enemies.
Out of confidence, he himself appointed Sūrya, his younger brother, as his deputy;
yet that Kucakrika, lusting after enjoyments, conceived a thought of malice.
Having committed an offense against his elder brother, that lord of the earth was afraid of the lord of the waves;
thus, the sun entered the orb of the moon with the desire to rise.
At that terrible time of battle, Bhūbhānu then closed his eyes simultaneously with the wondrous sun and moon, just as Rāhu eclipses them.
Then Tuṅga, the lord of Śamālā, who out of pride was casting his gaze toward the side of the sun,
was brought to a state of subordination by the King, who had already set out on his expedition.
Wandering through paths devoid of moon and sun like a thief in the night, the sun was abandoned by the courtesans; then, having been captured by the king, he was executed.
While that lord was personally seizing the opportunity to protect his own sovereignty,
the sons of Kalhaṇa, acting as thieves, instilled fear in him from snakes.
Then that king, having lost all hope while his kinsmen were still powerful,
sought refuge with the lord of Rājapurī, who was both learned and beloved.
When that wielder of the staff had gone far away, the jackals,
drinking blood, quickly devoured even the entrails of the people until nothing remained.
That food, abandoned by King Sumanas and defiled by the touch of the twice-born,
became for a long time the royal meal of the Dāmaras and Ḍombas.
Then, as his own realm fell into decay, what king— whose new rise was imminent— did not welcome him as he entered the supreme realm?
By personally conquering his enemies in battle within the royal city and protecting the descendants of Kahlana due to their Brahminhood, he obtained both the kingdom and merit.
That lord of the people constructed at Vijayeśvara a magnificent hall of twenty-one bays for the residence of cows and brahmins.
To his enemies, who were like thieves intent on plundering the schemes of Kālaṇa,
that lord of the earth was as loathsome as a lamp is to robbers.
That King Kalpadruma of poets, whose branches extended to the ends of the quarters, has been cut down by the sons of Kalhaṇa, who are ill-intentioned and possessed of wicked desires.
Making that king his central hero, the poet Paṇḍitayāśaska brought the vine of his own composition to the state of an ornament for the necks of the learned.
Having enjoyed the earth for sixteen years and ten days, he passed away;
then Jagadbhadra [ruled] on the fifth day of the month of Bhādrapada in his twenty-eighth year.
9) Rāmadeva (LS 4328–4349): Then Rāmadeva, his son, having slain those who had murdered his father,
entrusted the entire burden of the subjects to Pṛthvīrāja.
On the southern bank of the Ladarī river,
that lord of the earth constructed a fortress marked with his own name, like another mass of his own glory.
Having brought about his defeat through negligence during his endeavor for the conquest of Śamālā,
he renovated the temple of Viṣṇu in Utpalapura.
In the month of Vaiśākha, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth day— white as the moon— with devotion, in my thirtieth year, while King Rāma was protecting the earth, his beloved, on a Monday.
At the time of his victory over Śamālā, Pṛthvīrāja restored Murāri, who had been broken by bandits,
to a state of complete limbs and established him in the city of Utpalapura.
Alas! The Creator has failed to produce for that king the flower of the sandalwood tree, the fruit of the campaka tree, or even an offspring.
That king took as his son-in-law the son named Lakṣmaṇa of a certain Brāhmaṇa residing in Bhiṣāyaka.
A vast affection, like a painting of a fitting subject, far surpassed their own natural, unartificial father-and-son love.
The goddess named Śrīsamudrā, who had given birth to a son who was like the ocean,
established a monastery within the city on the Vitastā, marked with her own name.
Having ruled the earth for thirteen months and twenty-one years,
he himself ascended to heaven in his forty-ninth year.
10) Lakṣmadeva: Then Lakṣmadeva, overwhelmed by his limbs being torn asunder,
somehow supported that earth, which was like a thorny creeper.
Even though he was made a Kṣatriya, the king who was himself a twice-born did not abandon his own duty;
for even a stone, once dyed red, never truly assumes the luster of a ruby.
On the bank of the Vitastā, near the convent of her mother-in-law,
Queen Ahalyā constructed a new monastery, free from mud and inscribed with her own name.
Then, having gone outside to the circle with soot from Turuṣka,
the sight of the subjects was destroyed by the impure, flowing tear.
Having enjoyed [the kingdom] for thirteen years, three months, and twelve days, the king then passed away at the end of the month of Pauṣa in his sixty-second year.
11) Because of that harassment by Kajjala, Siṃhadeva was left with Ledarī as his sole leader;
then King Siṃhadeva was shaken by Saṅgrāmacandra.
Having established a monastery within the city, when Laharendra had passed away,
Siṃhadeva, a lion among men, then protected the earth which was distressed by decay.
Then the virtuous Siṃhadeva, accompanied by his preceptor Siṃha, performed the consecration of Nṛsiṃha at Dhyānoḍḍāra under the astrological sign of Leo.
The agent, the action, the moment, the preceptor, and the lion—these are known by the wise;
for him, this lineage of lions shall fall away from his vow.
Bathing Vijayeśvara for a single day with milk purchased for one hundred thousand pieces of gold, the king attained purity through his vow.
The king honored his preceptor Śrī Śaṅkarasvāmin, the instructor of mantras,
with the emoluments of sovereignty over eighteen monasteries.
The king always recited this verse, composed by himself as a gift for the Goddess of Speech, which served as the means for conquering the next world immediately upon rising from bed.
I bow to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gaurī, whose vision is as pure as fire, whose feet are worshipped by hosts of gods,
and who is adorned with the crescent moon as his mirror.
For the sake of giving water to travelers, for the libation of the ancestors,
for the destruction of the sins of husband and wife, and for the increase of merit; JRt_B.131 //
At the edge of Maḍava-āśrama village, Gaurī, the consort of Śaṅkara, constructed a watering place on the road by giving her own ornaments.
The daughter of Prajñadvija was the wife of Khonamoṣādhipa;
endowed with truthfulness and virtuous character, she was devoted to him as Gaurī is to Śaṅkara.
The punishment that had fallen upon the father due to the misconduct of his daughter was averted by King [Śibi], who was entreated by the dancer Iḍāgali.
Abandoned by the wisdom of the orthodox due to his embrace of wicked men,
he beheld his own reflection in the mirror of passion within the foster-daughter of the Earth.
The one named Darya, the husband of his sister, who had augmented the *Kāmasūtra*,
treacherously killed him whose subjects were disaffected and whose discipline was abandoned.
Having ruled for fourteen years, six months, and three days less,
the lord of the earth ascended to heaven in his seventy-seventh year.
12) Sūhadeva:
Then his brother Sūhadeva, further strengthened by Kāmasūha,
brought the entire land of Kaśmīra under his control, even though he was dull-witted.
Having arrived from every direction out of a desire for a livelihood,
many took refuge with that protector of the earth, just as birds resort to a flowering tree.
Then,
for the sake of his livelihood, Laṅkāracakra also arrived from the Darad country with a vast retinue to the extensive realm of Kaśmīra, where he was destined for future sovereignty.
In the kingdom named Kramarājya, that leader of men, being restrained by his duty, granted the village of Trāha for the residence of that self-controlled ascetic.
On the border of Pañcagahvara, Pārtha became like another Pārtha;
his son was Babhruvāhana, who made Garbharapura his capital.
In his lineage was born Kuruśāha, upon the mountain of whose uplifted arm the Night took refuge under the guise of the calluses from the bowstring, seeking the bright luster of his fame.
"Kaśmīra is Pārvatī; the king there should be known as born from a portion of Hara"—as if to provide proof of this very fact, he possessed three eyes.
For in Kaśmīra, the lineage of Kuruśāha,
headed by the illustrious Śaṃśadīna, shall establish an empire renowned for its fame.
From him was born King Tāha, upon whose bow-string—
resting like a slender creeper— the sound repeatedly reached the very end of the Vedas.
From Śāhamera was born Bhānu, who was like a summer heat of his own valor;
by the tears of his enemies' wives, his fire of majesty blazed all the more.
Once, while that Śāhmira was dwelling in the forest,
hunting first and sleep afterwards deluded his vision.
"In Kāśmīra, the kingdom shall belong to you until the end of your lineage"—
with these words, like nectar, he was consecrated there by the Great Queen in a dream.
In the Śaka year measured by five fires and the sun (1355), specifically the year marked by nine and eight (98),
he then gradually entered Kaśmīra together with his retinue.
As he approached with his family, the king favored him generously by granting him a livelihood,
just as a mango tree favors a bee.
Then Ḍalacā, the commander-in-chief of King Karmasena’s army, arrived in Kaśmīra like a lion entering a deer’s den.
As if to bestow sovereignty over sixty thousand villages,
he carried that same number of thousands of cavalrymen in his own army.
Desiring to turn back the flow of wealth through his expenditure, the king,
though himself of dark complexion, inflicted punishment upon all classes alike.

When the Lord’s anger was provoked by the offense of accepting that gift, the Brāhmaṇas, who were present there, performed an improper rite of expiation consisting of oblations of their own vital breaths.
The curse that was uttered by the brahmins against the king through the suffering of the punishment—
the certain severance of his lineage— is surely the fruit of that very act.
At that very time, the enemies provoked by the Bhauttas known as the Kālamānyas treacherously slew my kinsman and a member of my own clan under the pretext of [a religious] rite.
In his own country, the son of a kinsman named Vakataṇya was killed.
Honorable and possessed of extraordinary intellect, he was a forest fire to the lineage of Mānya;
by fate, his son Riñcana alone remained.
Then, having bound those dull-witted ones with a firm knot using snake-headed *ṭakkas* joined by mantra-threads, he desired to conquer them.
Through the mouth of his messenger, he proclaimed to those assassins: "Choose me as your servant; I am one whose treasury is being plundered."
That Man-lion, his weapons concealed by the sands on the riverbank,
awaited them for the sake of their blood, and not for the drinking of the sheath.

Those who had come there, though formidable like beasts of prey and accustomed to the ways of time, were rendered as insignificant as blades of grass by the axe of Paraśurāma, which lay buried within the sand, even though they were unarmed.
Having washed away the impurity of the dust of treachery toward his father with the blood of his enemies, he fled to Kashmir along with his kinsmen out of fear of the many remaining foes.
Then, for the sake of diminishing the splendor of the full Rāmacandra,
that moon-like lord of the earth endured the rising of the blue-hued Rāhu in the form of a cloud in the western quarter.
The sun scorched the quarters with its rays like a black-pathed fire;
all the people of Kashmir attained the state of locusts.
When the eastern and western directions were blocked by the Ḍal and Cariñca [armies], many people from those regions went toward the western quarter and then toward the direction of Yama (the south).
Then, for the *puṃnāga* trees— laden with fruit and enjoying the shade— the fear of being swept away by the floodwaters below arose from the wind that was shattering them against the mountain.
Like a fledgling bird fallen from its perch,
the royal splendor of the people of Kashmir was carried away by the swift-moving Cilla, who stole it from the world.
Having obtained wealth like rainwater from the sale of Kashmiri people to the Tibetans,
the cloud of plunder then thundered, filling all the quarters of the sky.
[Ps-JRT 9] Then Dulucya, who covered the earth with the armies of Turuṣkas, Tājikas, and Mlecchas, reached the city like Agastya reaching the ocean.
Beholding him as he approached, like deer seeing a towering lion or birds seeing Garuḍa, the city-dwellers fled.
Bound by him like serpents by a mantra-master,
some who had fled entered mountain caves out of fear.
The king too remained hidden somewhere out of fear like an owl;
what then need be said of the other people living there?
The curse of the Brahmins upon kings has never proven fruitless;
for consumption accompanied by its characteristic marks does not turn back without having killed its victim.
Previously, people were made to pay through the intense pain of imprisonment for a hidden debt;
later, they were sold as slaves by the Turuṣkas to horses.
Some are pierced, others are bound, and some are thwarted by him;
like trees before a fire, some undergo burning, some withering, and others ruin.
Bound by the piercing of their collarbones with a single leather thong,
even the sight of one another’s faces became difficult for them to obtain.
Bound by the Mlecchas at every moment for the purpose of bringing fodder, fuel, and other provisions, they were not released, like mice caught by cats.
Those who felt revulsion toward food due to the fault of contact with a cat,
yet being bound by hunger, ate the leavings of barbarians and even the bones of cows.
Those who did not drink even a span-deep water muddied with silt were led by their captors into the deserts and drank copious amounts of urine due to extreme thirst.
"Where is the food of barbarians, and where is our lineage? Hunger is unbearable; what is the use of sacred learning?
Sleep has not yet come. Thus they thought within themselves as they traveled along the road.
Whether they were walking, standing, eating, or even conversing,
there was not a single moment when he did not accomplish their purpose.
Some people were taken captive by the Mlecchas, some by the Khaśas, others likewise by the Daradas, some by the Bhoṭṭas, and some by the Turuṣkas.
Others fled in a state of agitation from the fear of the Turuṣkas, abandoning food, wealth in the house, possessions in the forest, and even their kinsmen on the road.
Compassion, reverence, and pity for those unable to flee quickly—
the children, the elderly, and the women— these have been abandoned by those who fled.
Those who were hungry did not eat on the road, nor did those who were thirsty drink;
agitated by fear, they could see nothing else behind them.
Some out of hunger, some out of thirst, some out of fear, and others out of shame,
entered into the interiors of mountain caves and perished there from terror.
Hearing that they had entered the cave, those merciless Turuṣkas, desiring to drive them out, then placed smoke at the mouth of the cave.
Even today, the instability of character among those men ruined within by smoke is visible, as is the soot arising from the smoke at the mouth of the cave.
He committed an offense against the king among his subjects, yet he reaped the fruit of it:
"The gaze of women is fickle; their cheeks are bitten by their own teeth."
Then Ḍalca, having destroyed the entire region and being distressed by the fear of a widespread cold,
departed from Kaśmīra by way of Tārabala.
Like mice from the holes of a fortress, the people of Kashmir emerged once Dalacota had departed, leaving behind only those who had been taken captive.
At the end of the calamity caused by the *ḍal* and *acarākṣasa*, the son did not find his father, nor did the father find anyone; and the brothers did not find their brothers.
At that time, the land of Kaśmīra was, for the most part, like the beginning of creation: devoid of people, a field of barrenness, unfit for enjoyment, and overspread with *darbha* grass.
The moon, having eclipsed the capable [planets] with its brilliance, shone forth again;
while the darkness blinded the entire world, the women going to meet their lovers enjoyed their pleasure.
Desiring to gore with his horn the king who had been released from the mouth of the eclipse-demon Rāhu and was touching the peak of the mountain, the sun then left the western mountain.
Seeing the sun stationed on the peak of the Sky-Mountain (Asta) as it was setting,
who did not suspect that the King’s own end was drawing near?
As the king of hawks, who desired to seize the city as his prey, was about to abandon it,
Rāmacandra— the moon of his lineage— placed obstacles in his path at every step.
Then, out of a desire to sell silk within the fortress of Laharakoṭṭa,
Riñcana, who was daily intent on deceiving the Bhauṭṭas, dispatched [the messenger].
In the same way, when the Bhoṭṭa world was introduced into the midst of the waves,
it vomited forth the honey of Rāmacandra’s tears while casting aside its weapons.
Leaving behind that wish-fulfilling creeper of the garden of Rāmacandra’s lineage,
that mighty-armed one placed Koṭādevī upon his chest.
Then the king, out of fear of losing his royal fortune, abandoned the city;
for how can there be any sprout of prosperity for those consumed by the fire of a brahmin’s curse?
Then King Jambū, terrified, entered a cave at the edge of the forest;
for how could such a death come to a sinner who stood face-to-face in battle?
In battle, the king, a wondrous cloud to his enemies,
brought a drought upon the eyes of those twice-born who had inflicted punishment, by raining down showers of arrows.
For four months minus five days, and for nineteen years,
that royal demon devoured the earth under the pretext of protecting it.
13) Then the great deity, Prince Ratna (Śrīratnasuratrāṇa), rested the earth upon the window of his arm, for it was exhausted by misfortune and the upheavals of unstable conditions. (JRt_174)
Just as a person perceives everything previously seen once the darkness has vanished,
he beheld the entire region of Kaśmīra and the former royal splendor.
Those who remained steadfast in their beauty like lamps at a festival were shaken by the powerful wind at the king's dawn.
When a breach was made by the needle of her mantra and it entered the thread of Bāṇa’s arrow,
it was a marvel that Lavanya’s neck then became utterly slackened.
Just as a bird moving through the sky might become distressed when landing upon a thorny branch in the forest, so too did the king become agitated while traversing that very region of the sky.
In that king, who was skillful in courtesy, forbearance was not observed even toward a son, a minister, or a friend when they were wicked, for the sake of the welfare of his subjects.
Once, while cutting down those enemies of unsubstantial nature whose glory was surging forth, he—
who possessed a royal umbrella— underwent a snapping of his [sword’s] hilt.
Ṭakkabhrātṛ’s brother, named Timira, exhausted by the heat on the road,
forcibly drank milk from a cowherd’s daughter in a certain village.
Then, having been questioned by the king who had been informed [of the matter], Timi, out of fear, immediately made a denial of everything regarding the cowherd’s wife.
When the cowherd woman, though situated in untruth, did not falter due to her fortitude, he,
who perceives the truth alone, split open the belly of the fish as if it were a vessel for wine.
As a stream of milk issued forth from his split stomach,
the King’s fame, the beauty of his face, and Gopī all attained clarity.
In a certain forest region,
two young colts, exactly alike, lived for some time on the grass belonging to two gatekeepers.
One of those two, whose offspring had been devoured by a lion,
felt such affection for the horse due to its resemblance [to her child] that she wished to adopt it as her own son.
"Is this mine? Is this mine?"—with such uncertainty arising, the two lords of the mares went before the king out of agitation.
Having heard their dispute,
the king then had both the mare and the colt brought before him by his own men.
As that colt ran playfully far away out of youthful exuberance,
his mother and nurse, becoming exceedingly disaffected, urged him on with goads.
While the members of the assembly remained silent and the two disputants were ready for the fray,
he brought a horse with its foal into the midst of the Vitastā river.
When the king of great intelligence had forcibly cast the young horse into the river from the boat,
his mother followed after him in haste and neighed most loudly.
When that king brought certainty to those very matters of doubtful conduct, the people thought that the Kṛta Yuga had arrived.
When the lord of men requested Śaiva initiation from the venerable Devasvāmin, the latter did not accept him because he was a Bhauṭṭa, fearing that he was therefore unworthy.
Through his steadfast devotion to the single vow of truth, the king’s younger brother, son, kinsman, minister, companion, and friend became a lord of serpents.
The king abandoned the serpent, but he did not again abandon what had been done by the serpent;
for it is the mind that destroys what is produced by the body, but the body does not destroy what has been done by the mind.
When the moon, the repository of digits and essence of nectar, became a serpent to the sun of the earthly realm,
his radiance was eclipsed, yet it severed the darkness of the worlds that could not otherwise be cut.
He who was dispatched by the king with a grant of wealth in order to turn back [the monk] who desired to enter Kaśmīra directly by means of a bribe— [Ps-JRT 11].
Then, once Dulucya had entered after taking leave, Udyānadeva, having found an opportunity, fled out of fear to the land of Gāndhāra.
Then the illustrious Udyānadeva, stationed in Gāndhāra and intent on striking at the vulnerable points, gave orders to the Ṭakkas and others out of fear.
I know that even while they are still living, they must go to that other city where a master who lacks discernment is served out of a desire for honor.
The serpent enjoys the fortune acquired by you at the risk of your very lives;
while his two hands labor with effort, his tongue partakes of the enjoyment.
The Lord, his limbs smeared with ashes, desires to turn a serpent into a necklace;
yet he displays a lack of regard for you, even though you are made of gold.
Making the fact that he was fed only milk his pretext, the king slew Timi,
suspecting him of possessing your own valor.
Thus, having been pierced by the message and stained with guilt, Ṭakka and the others once,
at Viṃśaprastha, then attacked the king.
By the falling blows of those sword-edges, the serpent extracted the heat of their own sovereignty from within their hearts; the kings merely fainted.
Then, considering themselves victorious and suppressing their anger at his death,
they went to another city, full of pride, in order to seize the kingdom.
Having remained for a moment as if dead out of fear of further slaughter,
and seeing his enemies gone far away, the king rose up once more for his kingdom.
As soon as they had entered the royal capital,
those of base intellect saw the lord of men returning, his fainting fit having passed.
"Was it not by you? Was it not by you?"—with such words, the foolish ministers, lacking in policy, were thrown into agitation at that time due to their mutual disputes regarding the king's death.
Due to their mutual anger and their mutual hurling [of insults],
those fools themselves brought about for the king the death he ought to have meted out to them in his royal palace.
Then the proud king, having elevated the remaining ill-behaved men to great heights by means of impaling them on stakes, sent them instead to the lowest state in every respect.
That wrathful king tore apart the women of his enemy's fortress who were with child,
using his swords as if they were fingernails plucking ripe *śimbī* pods from a field.
The pain arising from the anger of his enmity toward the king— caused by the slaughter of that royal family—
found peace in his mind, but not in his head from the blow of the sword.
Having seen that conduct of Ṭakka and the others like a bad dream, the earth instantly regained its tranquility through fearlessness, as if having awakened.
King Śāhamera, his mind serene, being situated in a state free from malice,
gave his own son Haidara, along with a treasury and a mother, for the sake of prosperity.
Nurtured by Queen Koṭī like a tree by the rainy season,
Śāhameru enjoyed her shade and her shimmering foliage.
Under the guise of a moat, the king constructed a city inscribed with his own name, which was surrounded on all sides by infamy born of his defeat.
The lord of the earth, resembling the sun emerging from the gloomy clouds of the month of Pauṣa,
once again brought light to the world for several months.
In the winter, due to the fault of cold and harshness,
the king’s head suffered intensely from a thickening caused by the provocation of the wind.
Although he always possessed the glory of qualities that alleviate the suffering of many noble beings,
the pain of the king’s own head increased to a great degree.
Then, on the eleventh day of the month of Pauṣa in the year marked by nine Nandas (999),
the king’s agony of death was dispelled by the physician of death.
Having protected the earth for three years less eleven days, King Riñcana departed for heaven.
14) Udyānadeva (LS 4399–4414) did not consecrate his son, named Haidara, out of childhood;
because he lacked such power, he himself was unable to govern the kingdom.
Because he was the lord of the clan,
the wise Śāhameraka had no hope of entering [the city] by means of his beauty, nor even by force, due to the resentment [of the citizens].
Then, together with Queen Śrīkoṭā, who was like the very embodiment of the goddess Jayā,
he caused that Udayanadeva to rule over the land of Kaśmīra.
The great swing of royal fortune, bound by its ropes of virtue, became heavy;
having abandoned its lofty position, the king fell from a high station to a low one.
Then the king gratified those two sons of Śāhmara, Jyaṃśira and Āleśira, by granting them sovereignty over the regions of Krama and Rājya respectively.
At that time, Queen Koṭā was like a wise counselor, the supreme authority;
the king, as if he were her very body, carried out everything she commanded.
Those [lamps] which had been eclipsed by the brilliance of the sun at dawn experienced their rising at that time, during the royal evening, through the light of their beauty.
When even the home of the gentle Saumya was invaded by his wife Koṭī,
why indeed should the invasion of his senses by beautiful women be lamented?
Avoiding the touch of the houses of Caṇḍālas in the land of Lāvanya,
he passed his time like a learned Vedic scholar through ritual bathing, ascetic penance, and the recitation of prayers.
How much religious faith can be attributed to that wearer of the saffron robe,
who tied a bell around the neck of his horse out of fear of crushing worms?
Bearing the very essence of wealth as an ornament for his treasury,
he presented a golden necklace with a crest-jewel to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Then Acala, arrogant because he had been granted an army by the foolish lord of Purasvāmin, entered Kaśmīra by force like another Ḍalhaṇa.
Having seized the earth by force with his own factions and cast down all directions,
that bull of the earth desired to break the mountains as if they were mere earthenware.
When that terrifying army had arrived, the lord of the earth, overcome by wretchedness and fear, quickly fled to the land of the Bhoṭṭas along with his troops.
"Withdraw your other army; why inflict such false suffering upon the country?
You must protect the kingless people of Kaśmīra like a lord of the clan."
Thus, having been deluded by the messengers dispatched by the illustrious Koṭyāmātya, Acala sent forth his army against Āsāra.

Having abandoned his own essential purpose and being devoid of substance, he was delayed on the road for some time by them under the pretext of a festival on the way, remaining steadfast [in his resolve].
Then, in order to protect the subjects, Queen Śrīkoṭyā appointed a Bhauṭṭa named Kheriñcana to the position of king.
Then, like a woman whose husband had died who had given birth to a stillborn child,
she of the steady intellect was grieved by all her own people after a long time.
Having made his days fruitful through the worship of the Śiva-liṅga with snow,
the fearless king returned from the land of the Bhaṭṭas to his own country.
Then, as if he were the full moon upon the mountain of sunrise,
he was respectfully borne upon the head by the Sun, who destroys the darkness with his rays.
The king gave up Jaṭṭa, whom Koṭā had borne to the minister named Bhikṣaṇaka, as his son Vardhana, just as one casts off death itself.
Then that hero Śāhamera, having protected Raiñcana,
became sightless due to the king’s excessive affection for his son.
Because of the queen's impartiality toward both sons,
Śāhmera, though hated by the king, did not touch him out of fear.
Fearing the upheaval and calamity of instability, the people took refuge with that king;
thus, he did not regard even the King of Śāhmera as being worth a blade of grass.
Having repeatedly shown the peacock to Śāhmira,
he terrified that royal bird excessively, day and night.
Protecting those standing on the banks, free from agitation and devoid of water,
that flood of the waters of Lord Alla caused his subjects to cross over in a marvel.
Both his grandsons, Śiraḥśāṭaka and Hinda—
heroes exalted by their virtues— adorned his lineage like the sun and the moon adorning the eastern quarter.
Arrogant because of his power over the gates, that Śāhmara was intent on defying the king’s command;
he became the gateway to calamity for those who served the monarch.
Having given his daughter to that lord of the land,
he conquered the city of Śrīśaṅkara and increased the king's apprehension.
Telākaśūra, who was under his control and a recipient of the sovereignty of Bhāṅgila,
became a man of action by taking the daughter of Jyaṃśiras into his hands.
Then that Nṛsiṃha, the conqueror of many forms, the treasury of fortune, and the abode of the imperishable, destroyed the army of the enemy, just as [the Man-Lion] destroyed the glory of the Daitya.
Possessing the depth of the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, and being the support for the Goddess of Victory,
that king of formidable splendor caused people to take hold of his hand in that formidable place.
Then Smerayaśas remembered King Kalaśadeva’s city of Vijayeśapura, which was burning here and there.
Having fashioned Mount Cakradhara as a support for his own discus to remain stable,
Śāhi displayed to the people the various functions of a mountain performed by Meru.
Bestowing the state of possessing all wealth and fortune upon Kampana, the lord who was his target,
he— possessing excellent fame— strangely obtained pure merit as if it were an immediate dowry.
Then, with the ambition of seizing the jewel of Śāhmira’s daughter, he captured Koṭarāja, that actor upon the stage of kings.
Some brought him into subjection through conciliation, others through force, others through gifts, and still others through fear;
thus the subjects of that fortunate king were blessed by his rule.
The world of beauty bore those daughters of his like garlands;
yet it did not realize they were female serpents with terrible venom, capable of taking life.
Because he was submissive to the seed of royalty, or because of his counsel and his valor,
what wild elephant among the Lavanyas did not come under the control of King Śāhi?
The king was overwhelmed on all sides by the flood of Śāhamera’s waters, which surged with the splendor of his desires, appearing like a tree situated in a heap of mud.
O Lord of the Earth, his life departed far away along with his pure fame, as if out of shame arising from his sovereignty over only a single city.
On the thirteenth day of Śivarātri, in the fourteenth year,
that patient king abandoned his forbearance, which had been defiled by the touch of Śāhmara.
That lord of the earth ruled over the territory of Kaśmīra for fifteen years, two months, and even two days.
15) Koṭā Devī (LS 4414–4415): Then, out of fear of Śāhmira, the illustrious Koṭā spent four days in secret concealment, hiding her true intentions and [the news of] the king’s death and other events.
"Let Śāhmera accept the empire through my son, and not through me";
thus, out of childishness, he set aside his elder brother and chose his younger son.
Then Queen Śrīkoṭā, deluded by affection for her son and by the infirmity of old age, did not wish for him to be confined.
Enhanced by her feminine nature and her kinship,
she herself consoled the earth, like a widow consoling her own female friend.
Then that queen, her fear dispelled on the first day of the bright fortnight,
caused the king to undergo his final sacrifice by means of his own elders.
Out of remembrance of her former kindness, all the ministers, including Śāhamera and the others, honored her as they would their own new crescent moon.
By her— who was pacifying all passion and was capable of removing the heat of affliction—
the subjects were made to flourish like creepers by a summer rain.
Fearing the loss of her husband’s life, the queen brought food for the mendicant monks in order to destroy that excessive hunger.
Then, having boarded that boat of wisdom, she crossed over to the further shore of her task amidst the floods of great fear that were otherwise difficult to traverse.
The inner strength of the Śālmali tree does not yield to begging;
for those possessed of pride cannot in any way endure equality with a shadow.
The characteristics of fire, such as smoke and heat, were present;
however, not a single sign of anger was observed in this wise man.
By the wise Śāhameru, afflicted with the disease of leprosy,
his own impending destruction was announced.
Then, for the purpose of investigating him, that illustrious Bhaṭṭabhikṣu was dispatched along with ten million [attendants] by the Goddess, together with Avatāra and the others.
The attendants at the gate barred entry to those followers who were disputing whether fomentation therapy is beneficial or not for aggravated *pitta*.
Those two, disguised as mendicants, entered his presence;
they were like deities protecting his life out of compassion, and not because of any sense of constraint.
Informed by his own attendants of their condition,
he, in due course, buried his swords in their bodies and extracted his own mental agonies.

Through their veins they immediately released blood, through their eyes vapor, and through all their limbs their life-breaths; those two released that hatred, and he [the king] released it from his mind.
He performed for those two a bath appropriate for liberation from disease, using their very blood as the wound-washing, the lamp-oil, the water for the full vessel, and the water for the half-vessel.
Both of these were intent on protecting Bhavānanda;
yet Fate, making one of them its instrument, carried off the other.
To pacify the torment arising from grief for a deceased twice-born man, a fool would further offer the life-breaths of others as oblations into his blazing fire of wrath. JRt_282 //
Although she was capable, the evil-minded ministers restrained Queen Koṭādevī from her desire to obstruct Śāhmara, diverting her mind from that course through their counsel.
Like a canal nourishing a field with its great abundance of water,
she— whose moonlight was the lotus of universal sovereignty— satisfied the world.
Once, due to a transgression of his command against the lord of Kampana,
she who possessed the luster of the moon and the lotus set out on an expedition, desiring to fight.
Then Kampaneśa, seizing her alive like a bird from its nest, brought her into the cage of prison.
The minister named Kumārabhaṭṭa, the preeminent among her counselors,
brought about a conflict with the other ministers through deceit for the sake of securing her release.
He placed a certain child seeking knowledge before him, who, though possessing a form similar [to that of the queen], was distinguished from her by his male state, and held a water-pot in his hand.
Having gone to the lord of Kampana, he, adorned by the praise of his wisdom,
addressed him with words endowed with excellence and nobility.
"O Lord, by soiling your own head at the command of a woman who is still alive,
you today fulfill our purpose regarding our manhood."
[Ps-JRT 14] Because she was a woman of timid heart, hostile to the festivals of giving and enjoyment,
great wealth remained with the queen’s kinsmen within the army.
Having gone to her prison at your command,
this person of yours wishes to restore the wealth to its master through both threats and conciliations.
Because she was a woman, she was unable to give it; since she had merely gathered wealth together, the Lord of Kampana, thus deluded, released him into prison.
Just as the queen was about to emerge from prison like a female *koṭā* bird,
at that very moment the twilight arrived, skilled in delighting the world.
Accompanied by a young student carrying water suitable for the twilight worship, he entered the prison,
and the queen's sorrows departed.
Having stationed that young student there, dressed in the attire of the queen,
he departed, taking with him Koṭā, who was likewise wearing her dress.
Even her guardians did not realize it for as long as she did;
thus, she made the lord of Kampana a mere elephant dunged by his own rutting elephant.
She was rescued from the begging of the master by the young Brahmin;
for what could not be achieved by another [who is] the slayer of the enemy with a single tusk, rather than by the elephant-faced one?
Although he was not driven away by her, Śāhvira did not abandon him out of fear;
for the wise, having incurred the enmity of one who is capable, do not remain indifferent.
She neither felt confidence nor was she provoked toward that powerful one;
for compassion, when joined with negligence, is the first sprout of destruction.
As the queen was relinquishing her residence, a mind intent on malice grew within her— rooted in wealth and passion— just as a poisonous creeper grows upon a *śālmali* tree.
For one side it was a source of growth, while for the other it brought about decline;
as it was for Koṭāśāha and Imrā, so it was for earth and wind.
While she was proceeding toward the city of Jayāpīḍa due to the demands of her mission,
that powerful Śāhameru once seized the city for himself.
When that powerful one had accepted the command of the world of beauty,
the queen, along with Jayā, closed the gate of the fortress in hope of victory.
For King Shāhmer, whose movement of the eyes had ceased, she became the sole cause of his fickleness, like a mouse that has entered a hole.
When the cave-dwelling clouds were suppressed by the powerful and wise Man-lion,
the serpents experienced constant fear, like a female jackal.

May the Queen grant me loftiness, free from any association with inauspiciousness, and a splendor exceedingly imperishable, through both the constituents of sovereignty and her own limbs which she has offered.
The queen would have cherished not only my sons,
but even their very lives, their sovereignty, and their praiseworthy succession of happiness.
May the Queen herself take her seat upon the lion-throne together with me, upon my chest together with Śrī, and within my heart together with Forgiveness.
Having thus diligently deluded that innocent girl with such messages and others,
the wise one took both Koṭakṣmā and Koṭādevī into his hand.
Having passed the night with her on a single bed,
he once rose in the morning and distressed the queen with harsh words.
Then, in the fifteenth year, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas,
that queen fell from her royal power like a star falling from the sky.
That leader of warriors, skilled in what must be done and like a wish-fulfilling tree for his kinsmen and relatives, bound those two sons as well.
16) To that Blessed One, the very act [of creation], homage be paid!

He is that Light whose splendor, stirred by the waves of the reckoning of space and time, unfolds when His own form is manifested on all sides by these sentient and insentient beings created by Himself.
Whether He be the Self, or Śiva, or Hari, or even Brahmā, or Buddha, or Jina—homage to that Blessed One.
Then he placed fear in the worlds of the low-born, fame in the quarters, the earth upon his arm,
prosperity upon his chest, and the goddess Kautī in prison.
Having brought the region of Kaśmīra to another state through the pacification of its misfortune,
the king bestowed upon himself another name, Śrī-Śaṃśadīna.

From him shone forth the king, a pearl-jewel from the oyster-shell of the earth which was the lake of virtuous wives; he was a wish-fulfilling gem for his subjects' needs and a diamond-jewel against the gems of his enemies.
Immediately thereafter, the calluses from the bowstring on his mighty arms, which were like kindling for the fire of his majesty, emitted smoke.
The king struck at his ministers, yet they did not pierce his doubt;
just as a diamond shatters other gems but cannot, in turn, pierce that very diamond.
Śrī Koṭā herself entrusted all her royal powers— which were difficult to bear due to her female nature—
to those who were worthy vessels of her trust.
Just as the sun dispels darkness from within a cave by its own majesty of light,
that king, having driven away the forest-dwellers who occupied royal positions from the royal precincts out of fear, shone with praiseworthy fame.
[Ps-JRT 21] There,
the movement of the Lord’s radiance was obstructed by his powerful forces, as if by the loveliness of twilight heat or by the darknesses of dusk.
And the realm of Kaśmīra was brought under his control in an instant by him, who punished his enemies with fierce valor, as if it had passed to him through hereditary succession. (b 358a-h)
Then, even by his prosperity, he caused a trembling as if it were plucked from his very heart,
through the other arm of the world and its other eye.
Having long since entrusted the burden of governance to his two sons, who were no less than himself,
the king, whose fame was exalted by his statesmanship, enjoyed the kingdom in happiness.
Having enjoyed the earth for three years and five days,
that lord of the world passed away on the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha in his eighteenth year.
17) *Gamshīd* (LS 4418–4420): Then,
having been unanimously commanded by the neighboring vassals,
that Jyaṃśira— whose splendor was undiminished— undertook the protection of the earth, which is like a lake of virtuous women.
The younger brother of the lord of the earth became an object of suspicion because of his two pillars— the strength and the intellect— which supported the archway of the kingdom.
For he did not perform any deficiency for the king; indeed, he neither withheld gifts nor took them, neither restrained nor favored, neither stayed away nor failed to provide sustenance.
The Great King surpassed his crown princes— who were endowed with excellence in learning, courtesy, discernment, and wisdom— solely by virtue of his age.
When the king failed to restore his former state of trust,
the crown prince, his mind alienated, made a slight show of indifference toward those standing near him.
Then, taking advantage of the opening provided by hearing that account of his despondency,
the royal officers immediately spoke to the crown prince.
When the conflict had become manifest due to his reliance on those acting as royal officials,
he, arrogant and relying upon them, went to the city of Avanti, which was their primary stronghold.
Then the king took up residence in Utpalapura together with his warriors, who were fierce in battle, and dispatched this verbal message to his brother.
If, due to the instigation of wicked people, you did not take account of my affection,
how could a trembling not arise from the fever of public scandal?
Reflecting upon the command of the king who has ascended to the third heaven— a command to be observed for the sake of mutual protection— bestow your compassion upon me once again.
Having thus instructed the messenger, that lord of men dispatched him,
and he sent forth his own son to slay the commander of Kampana.
He detained a messenger who reported that the crown prince had gone hunting;
meanwhile, Śrutadruha set out to slay his nephew.
"Why has the messenger not yet arrived? A very long time has passed," Lakṣmībhaṭṭa thought, agitated by anxiety, and went into the presence of the king.
And he said: "I know that your younger brother, having perceived your hostility, came here to kill your son; for which reason the messenger's arrival was delayed."
"Under the pretext that the crown prince is merely bathing, eating, and sleeping,

Once that city of Avanti has fallen into the hands of Śrīdevasaras, we shall immediately strike it as being leaderless; therefore, our victory is certain.
