For while he bears the royal parasols, the prowess of his enemies has been quelled.
The policy of that king caused the subjects to feel a dulled longing for former kings,
as his excellence surpassed them like sugar does the juices of sugarcane.
The established order of former kings was destroyed by him as he became new,
just as creepers struck by the cold season perish when spring arrives.
O Lord, by those who conquered even invincible enemies through mutual superiority,
his weapons were surpassed by mantras, and his mantras were surpassed by weapons.
Seeing that his body was occupied by loveliness, his face by speech, his chest by splendor, and his mind by forbearance,
Fame departed to a far distance, as if out of envy.
In the midst of the Kali age, the king’s righteous imperial system shone like an auspicious intermediate period (antardaśā) of the Kṛta Yuga.
Śrī Muhammadakhān, the brother of the Lord of Kaśmīra, was his companion in pleasures, his minister in statecraft, and his discerning guide in the determination of the scriptures.
What else could it have been? It was indeed the kingdom itself, though deprived of its parasol and fly-whisk, due to the power of Śrī Muhammadakhān, the lord of Kaśmīra.
Like springtime to the God of Love, the lord of Khuḥkara became a companion to the king; among his servants, he was the most beloved.
"Having warded off this state of disorder in this land ravaged by barbarians"—
thus he reflected upon the fruit of attaining sovereignty.
Meanwhile, those who had committed acts of treachery were clearly led away by the king’s favorites,
who were themselves free from fear, without even having consulted the protector of the earth.
Establishing fame in every direction, prosperity in the virtuous, and happiness among all people,
he brought about that breaking of the enemy's advance which utterly uprooted his foes.
The sun possesses exclusive intensity, while the moon possesses softness;
he, as it were, cultivated a splendor consisting of their union in order to conquer both.
How could I possibly describe his countless virtues here in this brief summary?
How indeed could a lord of elephants dwell within a cave of jackals?
Therefore, like the reflection of the sun’s orb upon a variegated mirror as vast as the king of mountains,
I shall place the narration of his virtues here within this mind, which is like the three worlds.
Just as heat and cold are equal at the onset of the seasons, and day and night are equal at the equinox,
his attitude was the same toward his own view or that of others.
Like a merchant who cannot tolerate an imbalance between the two pans of a scale, the king could by no means endure the loss of symmetry between his two eyes.
In that peaceful Siddhāśrama, the Brahmins were then no longer oppressed by the Turuṣkas— who inspired great fear— as they had been before, just as deer are not troubled by lions.
Then the sun-like lord of the earth caused those virtuous ones, whose state had been contracted by the moon-like Sūha who is a mine of faults, to expand once more.
Like a canal diverted by a mountain, that knowledge, having reached a downward course through the apertures,
was caused to flow forth by that virtuous man who was a lover of excellence.
Like a physician applying fire to sever a disease, the king gradually eradicated corruption and protected the virtuous conduct in Kaśmīra through his remedial measures.

The king, who was skilled in the application of the elixir of self-awareness, quelled the violent pride of his subjects, just as one pacifies the intense heat of the bodily elements through medical treatments.
The operation of the law of the fishes (mātsyanyāya) by powerful Time is the characteristic mark of this [king], who bears a portion of the splendor of the eight world-protectors.
For the purification of the earth defiled by contact with Sūhabhaṭṭa,
he surely kindled the fire of his majesty, which was like the blazing great sky.
As the king was accumulating the manifold web of counsel established in fivefold fashion, his host of enemies, as if out of a desire to conquer him, met their destruction.
While there is praise and celebration for the conquest of external, impermanent enemies,
on the contrary, there is reproach for Him who destroys the eternal enemy dwelling within.
Although he was capable, Indra, the lord of the Kāśyapīs, attacked only the Śakyas;
for the sun makes its journey through the sky when there are stars, but not when the moon is present.
That radiant one did not desire to conquer his enemies out of a thirst for power;
indeed, Hari does not slay elephants out of greed for their flesh and such.
On the mountains, his enemies surely resorted to the practice of the five fires as a penance for the exhaustion caused by the forest fire of the sun’s heat.
Though he was most exalted, he never once proceeded by a wrong path,
for the moon of the night does not ever rise except at the commencement of the night.
"Lest the residents, having grown arrogant, should fall into ruin by becoming impoverished"—
thinking thus, the king, who was learned in the science of polity, accepted tribute from them.
May Vairikīrti offer up his own self, along with his royal fortune, into the king’s majesty— which, united with prosperity, is like a fire fed by a gale— due to his separation from valor.
Once, when Jasratha was oppressed by the Lord of Delhi and had come to him for refuge,
he protected him within the mountain caves, just as a mountain protects the sun from the darkness.
While that ruler, the subduer of the wicked,
was governing the earth, there was a certain Brahmin residing in the presence of Jayāpīḍa.
Whether out of a desire for a mouthful of young grass or by the decree of the Creator,
the cow ascended from the depths like the embodied hope of those who consume the *svadhā* offerings.
Once, while he had gone to the kingdom of Maḍava for the sake of bathing at sacred fords,
that twice-born man recognized his own cow, with whom he shared a secret signal.
Having followed that cow as it went toward its home at evening with firm resolve,
he engaged in a dispute there with the master of the dwelling.
Seized by their resolve for greed, both of them, never ceasing their quarrels,
prepared to engage in a dispute within the assembly hall of the protector of the earth.
Since those two were unable to defeat each other in debate,
the king scattered grains of rice before a cow for the purpose of testing their skill at the crossroads.
Due to her practice of devouring [grass] since childhood, that cow, having quickly sniffed it with longing, ate it as if it were fruits; however, its offspring did not do so for long.
While the assembly was praising his royal skill, the king, having made up his mind,
punished the merchant with a fine by means of a twice-born man.
In that king, who was skilled in courtesy, forbearance was not observed toward a son, a minister, or a friend when they had become wicked, for the sake of the welfare of his subjects.
Even though he was beloved, the Yavana king Mereśāya was put to death by the monarch for killing his wife while intoxicated, even though she had committed no offense.
Casting aside all humiliation from the side of his enemies, that Indra among kings constantly showed honor toward the yogis who were skilled in the application of political strategy.
Valor and statesmanship, as well as compassion and discernment, shine within that king who rules over those monarchs.
Kāma always pays homage to the class of those separated from their lovers;
Smara, remaining free from transformation, has paid homage to the class of yogis.
In whom, who has newly united with her, both gentle and terrible qualities dwell;
where else but in the ocean have poison, nectar, water, and fire ever been seen together?
The seizure of wealth by litigants and defendants that had persisted for a long time was brought to an end by him, who acted with righteousness and followed the conduct of the virtuous.
Formerly, for some reason, a certain Brahmin named Laula sold one *prastha* out of ten *prasthas* of land, according to a written document.
Having proclaimed that [succession] to the children of Nonarāja and others while they were still infants,
Lāḷarāja thereafter attained absorption into Brahman in the year of his sale.
Because King Nonara and the others lacked the power [to resist],
the nine measures of grain were consumed by the powerful ones from there, even though they had not been sold.
When they had thus enjoyed ten prasthas for a long time,
those powerful ones devised a fraud regarding the sale deed in order to enjoy the mountain.
In order to facilitate the recognition of the form of the letter *e* situated at the head of the consonants,
scribes indeed drew a line to the left of the consonants and a stroke at their rear.
Due to changes in the script over time,
modern people, moreover, write a single stroke above the consonants that indicates the vowel *a*.
In the deed of sale stating, "One *bhūprastha* has been sold," there then appeared the line of the letter *e*, which is the realization of the letter *a* residing within the letter *ma*.
Those rogues who seized a *prastha* of land easily caused the letter *da* to be written;
they likewise quickly caused the letters *ma* and *śa* to be inscribed.
In the deed of sale, they wrote the syllables "one *prastha* of land has been sold," instead of writing "ten *prasthas* have been sold. (JRt_B.1033ab) 804ef.
While that king was deliberating, I challenged Nonarāja’s son in the royal assembly for seizing the earth by force.
Then, having had the birch-bark brought by his adversaries at the king's command, the monarch,
who was skilled in reasoning, read it while submerged within the water and cast it away.
When the nine new coins had vanished and the old ones remained fixed in place, he then made the courtiers declare: "A single *prastha* of land has been sold."
From that [act], the king obtained fame, the earth obtained a wondrous punishment for the deceitful,
the subjects obtained happiness, and the wicked obtained fear— all at once.
The moon causes fear to Rāhu at times; Time, filling its digits, brings about the agitation of lightning striking a tree; and the cloud, pouring down rain, gathers the distress of the forest.
So too, the Creator, exerting effort for the delight of all the worlds, momentarily produces an excess of fear in a virtuous man by showing him illness.
At one time, a painful eruption caused by poison afflicted the forearm of the king and the hearts of his subjects alike.

At that time, due to the affliction caused by the frost of the barbarians, there was no gain for the physicians of poison in this land, just as there is no flowering of blossoms in the month of Māgha.
Then Śivabhaṭṭa, a performer of sacrifices and a knower of the science of Garuḍa, was found here by the king’s followers who were searching for him, like a well discovered by travelers in a desert.
Though skilled in medical treatment, he hesitated out of fear of the barbarians;
like a man scorched by sparks, he touched the jewel only after a long time.
Having been granted immunity by the king himself,
Śivabhaṭṭa reached him and uprooted that poison-blast, just as an elephant uproots a poisonous tree.
When that single [wound] burst open, the king’s fame, the happiness of his subjects, and a continuous stream of joy— these three sprouted forth as it was ripped asunder.
Although the king, being pleased, offered him wealth according to his every desire,
Śivabhaṭṭa did not look upon it, just as one who has mastered himself does not gaze upon a beautiful woman.
[Ps-JRT 113] As if out of the force of its own burning and falling away, the merciless grass-fire, having consumed the grass, attains extinction;
yet, through the affectionate compassion of the arisen cloud, the luster of that very grass becomes once more a hundredfold more soft and beautiful.
Like clouds scattered by the month of Āṣāḍha as it intensely scorches the earth,
the Sūhabhaṭṭas, having been utterly withered, fled in all directions.
Like the rain-bearing wind, the king, eager for the conviction that comes from such knowledge,
summoned all those scholars to his own court.
In that region resembling a string of pearls, the leader placed the jewels of the learned, according to their merit, either by means of his splendor or his wisdom.
The king nourished the learned men whom he had planted by providing them with honor and sustenance,
just as a gardener nourishes trees with water.
Whatever had been destroyed by Sūhabhaṭṭa in the region of Kaśmīra was then restored by Śiryabhaṭṭa at the request of the king.
Having inaugurated the sacrificial processions and other rites for the Nāgas,
Bhaṭṭa Śiryaka bestowed upon the learned the lands that had been seized by the Turuṣkas.
When Udaya caused the tribute to be paid by him without fail to the Hindus,
all the Dānava-like Yavanas were enraged at Śiryabhaṭṭa.
At the confluence of the waters of the great lotus and the lord of serpents, he remained bound by the *kumbhaka* breath-retention like a leather bag, yet he continued to observe the Yavana lords.
The sun, whose heat inflames the mountains by day, becomes accessible even to the eye at evening; the moon, which causes its own rocks to wither during the day, makes the ocean swell at evening.

Having displayed his entire innate brilliance in the world by his own will out of mere compassion, he first [shows it] through the exhaustion of that person's fortune, and then, being great, he quickly withdraws it.
In the Kali age, overwhelmed by the touch and sight of sinful men,
the goddess Śāradā inevitably resorted to invisibility.
Perspiration on her face, trembling in her arm, and a burning sensation upon the touch of his foot occurred for the Queen now and then; yet at that time, such things had never happened before.
In the world of Kaśmīra, that goddess did not indeed remain intent on bestowing grace; she assigned a share [of wealth] only by her favor from riches acquired through treachery.
For the deities are indeed satisfied with even a mere blade of pure dūrvā grass;
they are never, however, pleased by lives defiled by impurity.
But in this Kali age, even that power of the Goddess has subsided;
nevertheless, the king once went with those on pilgrimage to see the Goddess.
Making the honey-sweet river productive through bathing and drinking,
he reached the autumnal field, which was crowded with a weary retinue.
Devoted to the Goddess, intent on granting fearlessness, and striving to manifest her power,
that king, who could discern between what was appropriate and inappropriate, entered there.
There too, seeing their wickedness, the king was astonished;
his devotion to the Goddess waned, and he became enraged at the pilgrims.
O Goddess, a direct vision of you is difficult to obtain even for the gods;
it should not be requested by us, who are stained by the age of Kali.
Out of compassion for those devoted to you who are unable to meditate upon or worship your partless form, you have assumed this form.
If your presence is not truly withdrawn from this image,
then let me behold you today in a dream, for that vision would purify me even more.
And so, we have served you there according to our ability;
yet, because of your wicked nature as a false devotee, you have gone far away from here.
"Why then are images reviled by the enemies of the Hindus?
Having been thus informed, the king, who had conquered his senses, [acted] on the seventh day of the month of Bhādrapada.
He lay upon the sacrificial ground within the temple of the autumnal field;
yet not even a single dream was shown that indicated his imminent presence.
In the ninety-eighth year of his reign, the Queen crushed her own image;
the Goddess certainly did not grant him her vision because of his association with barbarians.
It is a settled principle that a master becomes blameworthy through the transgression of his servants.
Indeed, there was nothing whatsoever that could interrupt his vision of the Goddess;
at that time, compassion, truth, and discernment took refuge in him alone.
Turning away from the Yavanas like a rain-cloud from forests, he,
impelled by an excess of joy, caused a great shower of gold to fall.
In that place where the weak were not punished as they deserved, except for thieves,
Bhaṭṭa Śiryaka attained the office of chief judge for the king.
Then, when there was no production of treasury wealth, the Bhaṭṭa made a vow,
threatening self-mutilation and the ruin of any speaker of falsehood.
As they raised their voices, filling the four quarters with the sound produced by the snapping of branches,
they were surely proclaiming their lack of Brahminhood at every step.
To protect those trees bent down by fruit and those people bowed by his virtues from being cut down, that victorious one provided fuel for fire.
Having abolished the triple staff,
he established the silver *māṣa* for the sake of preserving the caste of the twice-born.
When circles of people were killing cows with poison out of greed for their meat and other parts,
he prevented them by prohibiting the acceptance of vessels containing beef.

When her husband had died, she was about to go to another man as permitted by the kinsmen of her husband’s lineage; that highly intelligent king prevented her from such a lapse involving a Śūdra woman.
He prevented the disruption of the funeral rites for his daughters,
which had been carried out by greedy kinsmen of that lineage for a man who had died childless.
The study of the scriptures and other such pursuits had been destroyed for children by Sūhabhaṭṭa;
however, the learned Vidvān restored them once again by providing means of livelihood for scholars.
Desiring to manifest his own identity within the body of the twice-born,
the lord of the earth made a division between truth and righteousness under the pretext of a forehead mark.
In the first year of his reign over the villages, he, being intent on performing his duties, prohibited the imposition of fines for grain in the districts of *pattalās* and *ghoṣas*.
Having abolished long-standing frauds regarding weights and measures used for carts,
he established the prices of commodities on a monthly basis.
Having determined the price of goods brought from foreign lands in consideration of place, time, and other factors,
he cut through the confusion and plundered the day’s earnings.
Even the clever Śiryabhaṭṭa did not accept the fruit of a bribe;
rather, he accepted the imperishable fruit of merit resulting from his assistance during the rainy season.

For those seekers who desired the realization of the essence of knowledge, the fulfillment of that very wish occurred swiftly through the fruit of the king’s merit, even while [the deity] remained within his body.
The lordly king, from the mouth of the great Śrīśirya Bhaṭṭa,
dismissed the royal chamberlain named Dharmaprakāśa.
He warded off from afar that which was marked by words of definitive exclusion—
the bolt against the path of misconduct for future rulers of the earth.
That king, established in righteousness, settled the virtuous inhabitants in their respective towns; he restored wealth to those stationed at the village boundaries from the villages,
and that ruler provided for travelers in the forest from the lords of the wilderness.
Then, at every station, the laughter of the cremation-ground goddesses seemed directed toward Sūhabhaṭṭa, and the celestial chariots of the *pretas* shone forth.
The king, whose compassion was undiminished, rescued the earth oppressed by the Mlecchas,
just as Keśava gradually rescued it from the Dānavas.
Raising up the high ground and filling in the low ground,
that king made the earth free from unevenness for the purpose of sowing the seeds of his own fame.
This king’s vow of having no curiosity regarding the wives of others was broken only by his embracing the wealth of others.
Then, by the all-knowing King Samyagdaśabala,
the preceptor Tilaka was appointed to the highest office of the Sugata.
Śaśivabhaṭṭa Tilaka and Siṃhagaṇanāpati were the steps by which those twice-born ascended to their high positions.
Through the service of Brahmakuṇḍala, the Earth attained unbroken mastery in the aesthetic savor, just as Indra acquired the splendor of aesthetic flavor through his association with the cuckoo.
The illustrious Karpūrabhaṭṭa, who protected the lives of living beings,
made the assembly fragrant with his own virtues, serving as a refuge for the meritorious under the king's rule.
Knowing the position of the planet in the northern solstice from the movement of the planet in the previous [southern] solstice,
Ruyyabhaṭṭa was able to do so without the labor of calculation.
At every moment while examining the commentary and sub-commentary on the *Bhāṣya* by the venerable Śrī Rāmānanda, Sarasvatī gazes upon the earth with a bewildered mind.
The kings of Gāndhāra, Sindhu, Madra, and other lands became like common villagers, obedient to his commands, once that conqueror of enemies had subdued them.
Then, by his command, the king released Māladeva, the King of Madra, who had been defeated and captured in battle by Khukhurendra.
The king, skilled in statecraft, caused the king of Rājapurī to be overturned in battle in an instant by his own foot soldiers with a mere frown of his brow.
Having raised up the lord of Udabhāṇḍapura, who was supported by the King of Sindhu,
he struck him down again and again as if he were a ball.
Once, in the land of Gogga within the realm of Bhoṭṭa,
Mahīndra delighted the worlds with his virtues, like arrows released from the bowstring of a white-kneed archer.
When the command for rest was successfully carried out, the king, issuing a cruel order,
protected a golden image of the Buddha from the Yavanas.
Then his majesty, a touchstone for the gold of the Bhaṭṭas,
made the city of Malūta devoid of light through his prowess.
At that time, it was not only the hearts of the Bhauttas that became empty;
even their long-accumulated treasury was depleted due to the onset of fear of the king.
Bestowing upon his subjects whatever remained after their needs were met, according to what was appropriate,
the king performed an inspection of them, just as a farmer inspects his rice fields.
That bow could not even equal the Śārṅga or the Pināka;
yet, her brow’s state as a bow-bearer was superior, for it accomplished its purpose from afar.

Who could possibly equal the Sun, who always desires to forcibly lead the masses of darkness to their setting, and who, having replenished that waning moon with his own wealth, immediately causes it to flourish;
while the trees, by means of their branch-tops, merely provide space for the daughter of Kaśyapa [the lightning] and obstruct her with the weight of their rain?
The king banished that son of Laddarāja,
whom he had raised without taking anything from him, on the grounds that he was a traitor.
Once, a Yavana named Sadaula, having come from the region of Makkah and carrying a display of books, approached that king of kings.
The lord of men, who was fond of virtue, went every day to see him as he boasted of his own qualities, just as an ordinary person might approach another for the sake of a sight.
Through his investigation, that discerning king gradually perceived that the man was devoid of inner substance, just like a mere drum.
Like a father toward his son, that lord of the earth, an ocean of compassion, did not abandon his affection even for his son Mlecchamaskarin, though he was devoid of merit.
The abundance of his faults caused the subjects to tremble, like darkness at the onset of night or lightning amidst thick clouds.
At that moment, a certain king of yogins who had conquered his senses climbed upon a lofty pillar for the sake of attaining perfection in the practice of yoga.
While he remained without food for nine days atop a pillar, not even looking [at her],
the queen gave birth to a son for the king solely by virtue of his blessing.
While he was thus engaged in ascetic penance there, that ninth day for the king became no ordinary day,
but a great festival for the birth of a son.
At the end of winter, frost falls in the month of Phālguṇa; even for a lamp flickering beautifully, there is excessive burning at the time of its extinction.
An excess of cold prevails during the summer season, yet a cold object generally manifests its own nature as it approaches destruction.
Without having touched that armor of asceticism, he was sent downward by arrows,
as if to point out the future destiny of his assailant.
Beholding that man of royal honor becoming angry, the ascetic remained calm in mind;
he did not waver from his resolve out of fear, but rather out of adherence to right conduct.
Out of great fortitude, that high-minded one did not descend from the pillar;
nor did he, as a knower of yoga, immediately ascend to heaven, even though his gaze was fixed upon the world.
Saying, "Do not kill me, a guest on the path of yoga," the student was crushed by sword-strokes from the Mleccha ascetic.
Deluded by the intoxication of liquor and driven by excessive hatred upon seeing him,
that king, accompanied by the Mlecchas, struck the King of Yogins with arrows.
From the sight of him, tears hot, soiled, and copious fell from people onto the ground, as did reproaches toward the king.
Then the lord of the earth, having heard that, as if for the sake of purification,
plunged into the oceans of fear, shame, grief, anger, wonder, and anxiety over what had been done.
On that day, although his first son had been born, the king did not bathe, nor did he eat, nor engage in sexual intercourse, nor speak.
On another day, the king— who was skilled in questioning those who possess the knowledge of recollection—
was moved by compassion upon hearing that the punishment for the murderer was execution.
Having mounted him upon a donkey in reverse and wandering from shop to shop,
he was shorn while being sprinkled with human urine.
He prescribed spitting for all people, binding the arms with the entrails of a hungry ghost,
and a death-in-life as punishment for that emaciated man.
Flower-blossoms from heaven, devoid of wilting and carrying the fragrance of all directions, fell upon the king, as did the words of benediction from the citizens.
And that king begot four sons upon the daughter of the King of Madra,
just as King Daśaratha begot those [four] Janakas.
Jyāyān was Ādhamakhāna, and likewise another was Hājyakhāna;
Khāno was Jassaratha, and he who was known as Baharāma was Khāno.
Those who were severely oppressed by force by Hindava Sūhabhaṭṭa have gone to foreign lands, wearing the attire and customs of that region.
Constantly devoted to their own conduct, yet inwardly hostile to that conduct,
they were urged by the twice-born to practice their own way of life through force.
Those who, out of fear for their own protection,
were intent on offering bribes were restrained by the protector of the earth through the warding off of such afflictions.
After the churning of the ocean of milk, those jewels such as nectar were rendered useless because they could not be enjoyed;
yet it is said that Mount Mandara brought them to fruition through its gift to a worthy recipient—it is therefore praiseworthy among the ranks of the kings of mountains.
By causing rivers to fall into pits and making the fruits of the earth fruitless without water,
he brought them to fruition through his union [with her], thereby producing a wondrous fame.
Having caused the princess Vapriṇī to reach the land of Utpalapura,
the king found that her fault remained unaverted due to the futility of those two [earlier attempts].
Having caused a canal to descend from Mount Nandaśaila into the desert, the lord of the earth reminded the Wielder of the Discus, who dwells within the ocean.
Bearing a pure white fame that was not terrifying,
Karālamba caused the region known as Karāla— which is itself a subject of praise— to take on the appearance of a river-bank.
There, where the twice-born were recipients of land-grants and the women were likewise recipients of land-grants,
that city of the Jains was then built by King Karāla.
And in the land of Avantipura, the king, having heard news of his beloved,
caused canals to be constructed, resulting in an incomparable abundance of rice crops.
When the waters of the Gaṅgā were brought to Lake Mānasa by way of the mountain path, was this lake purified by those waters, or rather, were those waters purified by the lake?
Having created a reflection of its own form mirrored in the waters of that lake,
it made the city on its bank appear as if it were a double of itself.
Even the illustrious Sekandara Shāh became intensely frustrated and yearning, for his wisdom did not clearly flash forth to bring the illustrious Svaya here.
The illustrious Śrījainollābhadena, having brought that river Pahara,
poured it into his own city, turning a desert twenty *krośas* in extent into a lush land.
For those people whose minds were overwhelmed by famine,
a canal became renowned at every step as "Rest," because it produced rest for them under that very name.
The illustrious king, having joined forces with Pahara from Sūryapura on the banks of the Vitastā,
warded off the calamity of the enemy's heat.
From the edge of Mount Pradyumna up to the city of Amareśa,
he established a Jain city, enriched with monasteries, land-grants, and market-towns.
With its lofty stone mansions, it rose up as if to conquer heaven;
the serpent world descended there, having been transferred into the Jaina Gaṅgā.
The virtuous king, whose fame was radiant with smiles, caused the Jain Gaṅgā to be brought to the temple of Raṇasvāmī and forgot his curiosity regarding the footprints of Hari.
He founded the city named Jainagiri on the opposite bank of the Suyyā river;
it was adorned with palaces that seemed as if they were equal to Mount Kailāsa.
In the sacred field of Siddhakṣetra, at Sureśvarī, he— whose fame was radiant and who had subdued his enemies—
established the capital city named Siddhipurī.
On the summit of the palace, the king established two royal residences for Mārtaṇḍa and Amaranātha, which washed the distant sky with their white mansions.
It is said that in former times, Suyyarāja first caused this land to sprout with abundance;
and from that time until now, even though many kings have passed away.
Due to the meager merit of the subjects, it did not increase even slightly;
yet, through the power of his asceticism, it sprouted, blossomed, and likewise bore fruit.
That was performed simultaneously by the illustrious Jainaullābhadīna;
what greater proof could there be of the extreme purity of his ascetic practices?
While other rulers fall from their kingdoms upon the exhaustion of their prior merit,
the kingdom of that lord served as the means for him to attain kingship in another birth.
Having made the rivers his mothers and the earth the mother of the gods,
that lord of the earth constantly bestowed agrahāras upon the twice-born.
In Varāhakṣetra, Nagara, Vijayeśāna, Kādi, and other places,
he himself personally granted agrahāras, along with monasteries, to the Yavanas.
In Vijayakṣetra, Vārāhakṣetra, Śūrapura, and other such places,
he established sacrificial sessions and gave gifts, thereby causing even the Shatterer of Fortresses (Indra) to feel trepidation.
The King established a court of justice for the purpose of preventing the concealment of land and other property marked with signs that had been sold.
